directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Moudry fountain grass self-sows more readily than named seedless cultivars, so deadhead spent seed heads to control spread if that is a concern. Arching, medium-green foliage forms a tidy fountain-shaped clump topped in late summer by dense, bottlebrush-like flower spikes that emerge almost black before aging to dark purple-brown, a striking color rarely seen in ornamental grass seed heads and one of the darkest of any commonly grown fountain grass. Its compact size and bold, near-black plumes make it a strong textural and color accent at the front or middle of a border, contrasting well against lighter-colored companions. Cut the whole clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes each spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; blue moor grass tolerates poor, rocky, and calcareous soils better than richer garden ground.

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in well-drained, neutral to alkaline soil in full sun to partial shade; blue moor grass tolerates poor, rocky, and calcareous soils better than richer garden ground. Fine, narrow, evergreen leaves are blue-green on top and glossy dark green beneath, forming a low, dense, neat tuft that stays attractive through winter in mild climates, with small, dark, bottlebrush-like flower spikes appearing in early spring before most other grasses have even begun growing. Native to limestone grasslands and rocky slopes across Europe, it is a well-behaved, non-invasive clumper ideal for edging a border, rock garden, or dry shade under high canopy, tolerating both sun and part shade better than most true grasses. It needs little care beyond an occasional comb-out of old foliage and rarely requires division.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, average soil in partial to full shade; River Mist sea oats holds its variegation best out of hot afternoon sun and tolerates the same range of soils as the green species.

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in moist, average soil in partial to full shade; River Mist sea oats holds its variegation best out of hot afternoon sun and tolerates the same range of soils as the green species. Broad, bamboo-like leaves are crisply edged and streaked in creamy white, brightening shaded ground with a soft, luminous variegation before the plant sends up the same arching sprays of flat, oat-like seed heads in late summer that dangle and shimmer with the slightest breeze, aging from green to golden bronze. Like the straight native species, it self-sows in moist soil and can naturalize into drifts under trees, though seedlings of variegated cultivars often revert to plain green, so remove any all-green volunteers to maintain the display. Cut old foliage back in late winter before new shoots emerge in spring.

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun; African feather grass spreads by rhizome and can become aggressive in favorable, moist conditions, so site it where spread is acceptable or contain the roots. Narrow, upright foliage sends up tall, slender, densely bristled flower spikes in late summer that stand stiffly upright rather than nodding, aging from green to a pale straw-buff that catches low light beautifully and persists well into winter for cut and dried arrangements. Native to South Africa, it is a bolder, more upright counterpart to the more familiar dwarf fountain grass, useful for adding height and strong vertical structure at the back of a border or in a large container. Cut the clump back hard in late winter before new growth begins, and divide or contain the spreading rhizomes to keep it from crowding neighboring plants.

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Little Kitten maiden grass is one of the most compact miscanthus cultivars, well suited to small gardens and containers where full-sized miscanthus would be too large. Fine, narrow, arching green foliage forms a dense, dwarf mound rarely more than two feet tall, topped in fall by small, coppery-pink plumes typical of miscanthus but scaled down to match the plant's diminutive size. Its small stature makes it one of the few maiden grass cultivars genuinely appropriate for a small border, foundation planting, or large container, offering the classic miscanthus texture and fall plume display without overwhelming a limited space. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

directions: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Dewey Blue panicgrass is a dune-adapted selection that tolerates salt spray, wind, and drought better than most ornamental grasses. Broad, strikingly powder-blue foliage forms an upright, vase-shaped clump topped in late summer by airy, diffuse, pinkish-tan seed panicles that add fine textural contrast above the bold blue leaf color. Selected from wild coastal dune populations of the native seacoast panicgrass, it retains that parent's exceptional tolerance for salt spray, wind, sandy soil, and drought, making it one of the best ornamental grasses for a seaside or Gulf Coast dune-style landscape. It needs no supplemental irrigation once established and provides valuable erosion control and wildlife habitat value in coastal plantings; cut back in late winter before new growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Aureovariegata sedge is a classic, long-cultivated clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring; Aureovariegata sedge is a classic, long-cultivated clumper that neither runs nor self-sows aggressively. Arching, evergreen leaves are striped with a soft golden-yellow center bordered in green, a warmer, more golden variegation pattern than the white-edged sedge cultivars more commonly sold, brightening shaded ground with a sunny glow even on overcast days. One of the older gold-variegated Japanese sedge selections still in cultivation, it forms a neat, fountain-shaped mound useful as a border edger, container filler, or small-scale groundcover under high-canopy shade trees. Comb out old foliage by hand in late winter rather than shearing, and divide congested clumps in spring only when the center begins to thin.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database
